<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\index{signature}
A \textbf{signature} $\Phi$ is an object of $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}^\natural$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{def:term}
\index{term}
Let $n \in \natural$.
An \textbf{$n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term} is defined by the following inductive clauses:
\begin{itemize}
\item $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ are $n$-ary\ terms.
\item If $\phi \in \Phi_m$ and $t_1, \dots, t_m$ are $n$-ary\ terms, then $\phi
 (t_1, \dots, t_m)$ is an $n$-ary\ term.
\end{itemize}
A \textbf{$\Phi$-term} is an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term for some $n \in \natural$.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
\index{var}
Let $t$ be an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term.
Then $\mathop{\rm{var}}(t)$ is the sequence of elements of $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ given as
follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathop{\rm{var}}(x_i) = (x_i)$,
\item $\mathop{\rm{var}}(\phi  (t_1, \dots, t_n)) =
\mathop{\rm{var}}(t_1) \mathrel{++} \mathop{\rm{var}}(t_2) \mathrel{++} \dots \mathrel{++} \mathop{\rm{var}}(t_n)$,
\end{itemize}
where $\mathrel{++}$ is concatenation.
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\index{supp}
Let $t$ be an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term.
Then $\mathop{\rm{supp}}(t)$, the \textbf{support of $t$}, is the subset of $\{x_1, \dots,
x_n\}$ given as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathop{\rm{supp}}(x_i) = \{x_i\}$,
\item $\mathop{\rm{supp}}(\phi  (t_1, \dots, t_n)) =
\mathop{\rm{supp}}(t_1) \cup \mathop{\rm{supp}}(t_2) \cup \dots \cup \mathop{\rm{supp}}(t_n)$,
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\index{labelling function}
Let $t$ be an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term, with $\mathop{\rm{var}}(t) = (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m})$.
The \textbf{labelling function} $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$ of $t$ is the function ${\underline{m}} \to {\underline{n}}$
sending $j$ to $i_j$.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
\index{equation}
An \textbf{$n$-ary\ $\Phi$-equation} is a pair $(s,t)$ of $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-terms.
A \textbf{$\Phi$-equation} is an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-equation for some $n \in
\natural$.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
\label{def:sr_linterms}
\index{linear!term}\index{strongly regular!term}
An $n$-ary\ term $t$ is \textbf{linear} if $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$ is a bijection, and
\textbf{strongly regular} if $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$ is an identity.
\index{linear!equation}\index{strongly regular!equation}
An equation $(s,t)$ is \textbf{linear} if both $s$ and $t$ are linear, and
\textbf{strongly regular} if both $s$ and $t$ are strongly regular.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\index{presentation!of an algebraic theory}
A \textbf{presentation of a (one-sorted) algebraic theory} is 
\begin{itemize}
\item a signature $\Phi$,
\item a set $E$ of $\Phi$-equations.
\end{itemize}
\index{generating operation}
Elements of $\Phi_n$ are called ($n$-ary) \textbf{generating operations}.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
\index{linear!presentation}
\index{strongly regular!presentation}
Let $P = (\Phi, E)$ be a presentation of an algebraic theory.
$P$ is \textbf{linear} if every equation in $E$ is linear, and
\textbf{strongly regular} if every equation in $E$ is strongly regular.
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a signature}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature.
An \textbf{algebra} for $\Phi$ is
\begin{itemize}
\item a set $A$,
\item for each $n$-ary\ operation $\phi$, a map $\phi_A : A^n \to A$.
\index{primitive operation}
These are called the \textbf{primitive operations} of the algebra $A$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a presentation}
Let $P = (\Phi, E)$ be a presentation of an algebraic theory.
A \textbf{$P$-algebra} is a $\Phi$-algebra $A$ such that, for every equation
$(s,t)$ in $E$, the derived operations $s_A, t_A$ are equal.
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- defn-12: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of algebras for a signature}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature, and $A$ and $B$ be $\Phi$-algebras.
A \textbf{morphism of $\Phi$-algebras} $f : A \to B$ is a map $f:A \to B$
which commutes with every primitive operation:
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{f^n} \ar[d]_-{\phi_A}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{\phi_B} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{f}
		& B
	}

\]
for every $n \in \natural$ and every $n$-ary\ primitive operation $\phi$.
If $P = (\Phi, E)$ is a presentation, then a \textbf{morphism of
$P$-algebras} is a morphism of $\Phi$-algebras.
<!-- end defn-12 -->
<!-- defn-13: body_md -->
\index{grafting!of terms}
Let $t$ be an $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-term, and $t_1, \dots, t_n$ be $\Phi$-terms.
Then the \textbf{graft} $t (t_1, \dots, t_n)$ is the $\Phi$-term defined
recursively as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $t = x_i$, then $t (t_1, \dots, t_n) = t_i$.
\item If $t = \phi(s_1, \dots, s_m)$, where $\phi \in \Phi_m$ and $s_1, \dots,
s_m$ are $n$-ary\ $\Phi$-terms, then 

$t  (t_1, \dots, t_n)
	= \phi  ((s_1 (t_1, \dots, t_n)), \dots, s_m (t_1, \dots, t_n))$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-13 -->
<!-- defn-14: body_md -->
\index{closure}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature and $E$ be a set of $\Phi$-equations.
The \textbf{closure} $\bar E$ of $E$ is the smallest equivalence relation on
$\mathop{\rm{term}} \Phi$ which contains $E$ and is closed under grafting of terms:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $(s,t) \in \bar E$, then $(s  (t_1, \dots, t_n), t  (t_1, \dots, t_n)) \in \bar E$ for all $t_1, \dots, t_n$.
\item if $(s_i, t_i) \in \bar E$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, then $(t  (s_1,
\dots, s_n), t  (t_1, \dots, t_n)) \in \bar E$ for all $t$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-14 -->
<!-- defn-15: body_md -->
\label{def:clone}
\index{clone}
A \textbf{clone} $K$ is
\begin{itemize}
\item a sequence of sets $K_0, K_1, \dots$,
\item for all $m,n \in \natural$, a function $\bullet : K_n \times (K_m)^n \to
K_m$,
\item for each $n \in \natural$ and each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, an
element $\delta^i_n \in K_n$
\end{itemize}
such that
\begin{itemize}
\item for each $f \in K_n$, $g_1,\dots,g_n \in K_m$, $h_1, \dots, h_{m} \in
K_p$,
\[
f \bullet(g_1 \bullet (h_1, \dots, h_m), \dots, g_n \bullet (h_1, \dots,
h_m))
= (f \bullet (g_1, \dots, g_n)) \bullet (h_1, \dots, h_{m})
\]
\item for all $n$, all $i \in {1, \dots, n}$ and all $f_1, \dots, f_n \in K_m$,
\[
\delta^i_n \bullet (f_1, \dots, f_n) = f_i
\]
\item for all $n$ and $f \in K_n$,
\[
f \bullet (\delta_n^1, \dots, \delta_n^n) = f
\]
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-15 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\index{endomorphism clone}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be a finite product category, and $A$ be an object of \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}.
The \textbf{endomorphism clone} of $A$, $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$, is defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n = \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A^n, A)$ for each $n \in \natural$, 
\item for all $n \in \natural$ and $i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, the map
$\delta^i_n$ is the projection of $A^n$ onto its $i$th factor,
\item for all $n, m \in \natural$, all $f \in \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n$, and all $g_1, \dots,
g_n \in \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_m$, the morphism $f\bullet(g_1, \dots, g_n)$ is the composite
$fh$, where $h$ is the unique arrow $A^m \to A^n$ induced by the maps $g_1,
\dots, g_n$ and the universal property of $A^n$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- defn-16: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of clones}
A \textbf{morphism} of clones $f: K \to K'$ is a map in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}^\natural$
which commutes with the composition operations and $\delta$s.
<!-- end defn-16 -->
<!-- defn-17: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a clone}
Let $K$ be a clone, and \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ a finite product category with specified finite
powers.
An \textbf{algebra} for $K$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is an object $A \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ and a morphism of
clones $K \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$.
<!-- end defn-17 -->
<!-- defn-18: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of algebras for a clone}
Let $A$ and $B$ be algebras for a clone $K$ in a finite product category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$
with specified finite powers.
A \textbf{morphism} of algebras $A \to B$ is a morphism $F : A \to B$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\
such that the diagram
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{F^n} \ar[d]_-{\hat k}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{\hat k} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{F}
		& B
	}

\]
commutes for all $n \in \natural$ and all $k \in K_n$.
<!-- end defn-18 -->
<!-- defn-19: body_md -->
\index{Lawvere theory}
A \textbf{Lawvere theory} is a category $\mathcal{T}$ whose objects form a
denumerable set $\{\bf{0}, \bf{1}, \bf{2}, \dots \}$, such that $\bf{n}$ is the
$n$-th power of $\bf{1}$.
\index{morphism!of Lawvere theories}
A \textbf{morphism} of Lawvere theories $\mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{S}$ is an identity-on-objects
functor $\mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{S}$ which preserves projection maps.
The category of Lawvere theories and their morphisms is called $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Law}}}}$.
\index{\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Law}}}}}
An \textbf{algebra} for $\mathcal{T}$ is a functor $F:\mathcal{T} \to \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}$ which preserves
finite products.
\index{algebra!for a Lawvere theory}
A \textbf{morphism} of algebras is a natural transformation.
\index{morphism!of algebras for a Lawvere theory}
The \textbf{category of $\mathcal{T}$-algebras} is the full subcategory of $[\mathcal{T}, \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}]$
whose objects are finite-product-preserving functors.
<!-- end defn-19 -->
<!-- defn-20: body_md -->
\index{finite product theory, multi-sorted}
Let $S$ be a set.
An \textbf{$S$-sorted finite product theory} is a small finite product
category whose underlying monoidal category is strict and whose monoid of
objects is the free monoid on $S$.
Elements of $S$ will be called \textbf{sorts}.
Algebras and morphisms of algebras are defined as above.
<!-- end defn-20 -->
<!-- defn-21: body_md -->
\label{def:monad_morphism}
\index{morphism!of monads}
Let $(T_1, \mu_1, \eta_1), (T_2, \mu_2, \eta_2)$ be monads on a category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
A \textbf{morphism of monads} $(T_1, \mu_1, \eta_1) \to (T_2, \mu_2, \eta_2)$
is a natural transformation $\alpha : T_1 \to T_2$ such that the diagrams
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:monad_morph_mu}
\xymatrix{
	T_1^2 \ar[r]^{\mu_1} \ar[d]_{\alpha * \alpha} & T_1 \ar[d]^\alpha \\
	T_2^2 \ar[r]_{\mu_2} & T_2
}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:monad_morph_eta}
\xymatrix{
	1 \ar[r]^{\eta_1} \ar[dr]_{\eta_2} & T_1 \ar[d]^{\alpha} \\
	& T_2
}
\end{equation}
commute.
<!-- end defn-21 -->
<!-- defn-22: body_md -->
\index{filtered!category}
A category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is \textbf{filtered} if every finite diagram in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ admits a
cocone.
<!-- end defn-22 -->
<!-- defn-23: body_md -->
\index{filtered!colimit}
A \textbf{filtered colimit} in a category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is the colimit of a diagram $D: \I \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, where $\I$ is a filtered category.
<!-- end defn-23 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Every object in \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}\ is a filtered colimit of finite sets.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $X \in \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}$, and consider the subcategory $\I$ of $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}$ whose objects are
finite subsets of $X$ and whose morphisms are inclusions.
This is a directed poset, and thus a filtered category.
$X$ is the colimit of the inclusion of $\I$ into $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let $\I$ be a small category.
Colimits of shape $\I$ in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}$ commute with all finite limits iff $\I$ is
filtered.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See \cite{m+m}, Corollary VII.6.5.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defn-24: body_md -->
\index{finitary!functor}
A functor $F: \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}} \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}$ is \textbf{finitary} if it preserves filtered
colimits.
<!-- end defn-24 -->
<!-- defn-25: body_md -->
\index{finitary!monad}
A monad $(T, \mu, \eta)$ on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is \textbf{finitary} if $T$ is finitary.
<!-- end defn-25 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a clone. 
Then $K_{(\Phi_K, E_K)}$ is isomorphic to $K$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
See \cite{johnstone}, Lemma 1.7.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Let $(\Phi, E)$ be a presentation of an algebraic theory.
Let $(\Phi', E')$ be the presentation obtained from the clone $K_{(\Phi, E)}$.
Then the category $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(\Phi, E)$}}}}$ is isomorphic to the category $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(\Phi',
E')$}}}}$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
See \cite{johnstone}, Lemma 1.8.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- defn-26: body_md -->
\index{linear!clone}
\index{strongly regular!clone}
Let $K$ be a clone.
We say that $K$ is \textbf{strongly regular} (resp. \textbf{linear}) if
there exists a strongly regular (resp. linear) presentation $P$ such that
$K = K_{(\Phi, E)}$.
<!-- end defn-26 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a clone.
Then $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(K)$}}}} \simeq \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(\mathcal{T}_K)$}}}}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $K$-algebra.
We define a $\mathcal{T}_K$-algebra $F_A$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $F_A {\bf n} = A^n$ for all $n \in \natural$;
\item If $k \in \mathcal{T}_K({\bf n}, 1) = K_n$, then $F_Ak = \hat k$;
\item if $(k_1, \dots, k_n) : {\bf m} \to {\bf n}$ in $\mathcal{T}_K$, then 
$F_A (k_1, \dots, k_n)$ is the unique arrow $A^m \to A^n$ such that the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
	& A^m \ar[ddl]_{\widehat k_1} \ar[ddr]^{\widehat k_n} \ar@{..>}[d] \\
	& A^n \ar[dl]^{\widehat{\delta^1_n}} \ar[dr]_{\widehat{\delta_n^n}} \\
	A & \dots & A
}
\]
commutes.
\end{itemize}
Let $f : A \to B$ be a morphism of $K$-algebras.
Then the diagram
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{f^n} \ar[d]_-{\widehat k}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{\widehat k} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{f}
		& B
	}

\]
commutes for all $n \in \natural$ and all $k \in K_n$.
By the universal property of $B^m$, the diagram
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{f^n} \ar[d]_-{F_A(k_1, \dots, k_m)}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{F_B(k_1, \dots, k_m)} \\
		A^m \ar[r]^-{f^m}
		& B^m
	}

\]
commutes for all $n, m \in \natural$ and all $(k_1, \dots, k_m) : {\bf n} \to {\bf m}$ in $\mathcal{T}_K$.
Hence $F_f = (f^n)_{{\bf n}}$ is a natural transformation $F_A \to F_B$, and
hence a morphism of $\mathcal{T}_K$-algebras.
This defines a functor $F_{(-)} : \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(K)$}}}} \to \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(\mathcal{T}_K)$}}}}$; we wish to show that
it is an equivalence.

For every $\mathcal{T}_K$-algebra $G$, we may define a $K$-algebra $A$ by setting $A =
G{\bf 1}$ and $\hat k = G({\bf n} \stackrel{k}{\longrightarrow} {\bf 1})$ for
all $k \in K_n$ and all $n \in \natural$.
Then $F_A$ is isomorphic as a $\mathcal{T}_K$-algebra to $G$, and hence the functor
$F_{(-)} : \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(K)$}}}} \to \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(\mathcal{T}_K)$}}}}$ is essentially surjective on objects.
We shall show further that it is full and faithful.
Let $A$ and $B$ be $K$-algebras, and let $\alpha_n : F_A \to F_B$ be
a morphism between their associated $\mathcal{T}_K$-algebras.
Since the diagram
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{\alpha_n} \ar[d]_-{\widehat{\delta^i_n}}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{\widehat{\delta^i_n}} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{\alpha_1}
		& B
	}

\]
commutes for all $n \in \natural$ and all $i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, it must be
the case that $\alpha_n = \alpha_1^n$ for all $n$.
Hence, the diagram
\[

	\xymatrix{
		A^n \ar[r]^-{\alpha_1^n} \ar[d]_-{\widehat k}
		& B^n \ar[d]^-{\widehat k} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{\alpha_1}
		& B
	}

\]
must commute for all $n \in \natural$ and all $k \in K_n$.
So $\alpha_1$ is a $K$-algebra morphism, and $\alpha_n = F_{\alpha_1}$.
Hence $F_{(-)}$ is full.
Suppose $F_f = F_g$; then $(F_f)_{\bf 1} = (F_g)_{\bf 1}$, so $f = g$.
Hence $F_{(-)}$ is faithful; and hence it is an equivalence of categories.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
The functor $K_{(-)}$ is pseudo-inverse to the functor $\mathcal{T}_{(-)}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Since every object in a Lawvere theory is a copower of ${\bf 1}$, a Lawvere
theory $\mathcal{T}$ is entirely determined (up to isomorphism) by the hom-sets $\mathcal{T}({\bf
n}, {\bf 1})$, and thus by $K_\mathcal{T}$.
The theorem follows straightforwardly.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
The monad so constructed is finitary.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
See \cite{a+r}, Theorems 3.18 and 1.5, and Remarks 3.4(4) and 3.6(6).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- defn-27: body_md -->
\index{multicategory!plain}
A \textbf{plain multicategory} (or simply ``multicategory'') $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$
consists of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item a collection $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_0$ of \emph{objects},
\item for all $n \in \natural$ and all $c_1, \dots, c_n,
d \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_0$, a set of \emph{arrows} $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c_1, \dots, c_n; d)$,
\item for all $n, k_1, \dots k_n \in \natural$ and $c_1^1 \dots, c_{k_n}^n,
d_1, \dots, d_n, e \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_0$, a function called \emph{composition}
\[\circ
: \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(d_1, \dots, d_n;e)  \times
\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c^1_1, \dots, c^1_{k_1};d_1) \times \dots \times
\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c^n_1, \dots, c^n_{k_n};d_n)
\to
\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c^1_1, \dots, c^n_{k_n};e)\]
\item for all $c \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, an \emph{identity arrow} $1_c \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c;c)$
\end{itemize}
satisfying the following axioms:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Associativity:} $f \circ (g_\bullet \circ h_\bullet^\bullet) = (f \circ g_\bullet)
\circ h_\bullet^\bullet$ wherever this makes sense (we borrow the ${}_\bullet$ notation for
sequences from chain complexes)
\item \emph{Units:} $1 \circ f = f = f \circ (1, \dots, 1)$ for all $f$.
\end{itemize}
A plain multicategory \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is \textbf{small} if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_0$ forms a set.
In line with the definition above, we shall take all our multicategories to be
locally small: this restriction is not essential.
<!-- end defn-27 -->
<!-- defn-28: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of plain multicategories}
A \textbf{morphism} of multicategories $F: \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}} \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}$ is a map $F : \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_0
\to \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}_0$ together with maps $F : \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(c_1, \dots, c_n ; c) \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}(F c_1,
\dots, F c_n ; F c)$ which commute with $\circ$ and identities.
\index{transformation!between morphisms of plain multicategories}
A \textbf{transformation} of multicategory maps $\alpha : F \to G$ is a family
of arrows $\alpha_c \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}(F c ; G c)$, one for each $c \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, satisfying the
analogue of the usual naturality squares: for all maps $f: c_1, \dots, c_k \to
c$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}, we must have
\[
\alpha_c \circ Ff = Gf \circ (\alpha_{c_1}, \dots, \alpha_{c_k})
\]
<!-- end defn-28 -->
<!-- defn-29: body_md -->
\label{def:umoncat}
\index{unbiased!monoidal category}
An \textbf{unbiased weak monoidal category} $(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}, \otimes, \gamma, \iota)$
consists of
\begin{itemize}
\item a category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$,
\item for each $n \in \natural$, a functor $\otimes_n : \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}^n \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ called \textbf{$n$-fold tensor} and written
\[
(a_1, \dots, a_n) \mapsto (a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n)
\]
\item for each $n, k_1, \dots, k_n \in \natural$, a natural isomorphism
\[
\gamma : \otimes_n \circ (\otimes_{k_1} \times \dots \times \otimes_{k_n})
\longrightarrow \otimes_{\sum k_i}
\]
\item a natural isomorphism
\[
\iota: 1_A \to \otimes_1
\]
\end{itemize}
satisfying
\begin{itemize}
\item associativity: for any triple sequence $a^\bullet_{\bullet\bullet}$ of objects in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, the
diagram
\[
\xymatrixrowsep{4pc}
\xymatrixcolsep{-10pc}
\xymatrix{
&(
((\otimes a_{1 1}^\bullet) \otimes \dots \otimes (\otimes a_{1 k_1}^\bullet))
\otimes \dots \otimes
((\otimes a_{n 1}^\bullet) \otimes \dots \otimes (\otimes a_{n k_n}^\bullet)))
\ar[dl] \ar[dr] \\
((\otimes a_{1 \bullet}^\bullet)
\otimes \dots \otimes
(\otimes a_{n \bullet}^\bullet))
\ar[dr]
& & ((\otimes a_{1 1}^\bullet) \otimes \dots \otimes
(\otimes a_{n k_n}^\bullet))
\ar[dl] \\
& (a_{1 1}^1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_{n k_n}^{m_{k_n}})
}
\]
commutes.
\item identity: for any $n \in \natural$ and any sequence $a_1, \dots, a_n$ of
objects in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, the diagrams
\[
\xymatrixcolsep{4pc}
\xymatrixrowsep{4pc}
\xymatrix{
(a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n) \ar[r]^{(\iota\otimes\dots\otimes\iota)}
\ar[dr]_1
& ((a_1) \otimes \dots \otimes (a_n)) \ar[d]^\gamma \\
& (a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n)
}
\]
\[
\xymatrixcolsep{4pc}
\xymatrixrowsep{4pc}
\xymatrix{
(a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n) \ar[r]^{\iota}
\ar[dr]_1
& ((a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n)) \ar[d]^\gamma \\
& (a_1 \otimes \dots \otimes a_n)
}
\]
commute.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-29 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\index{multicategory!underlying multicategory of a monoidal category}
\index{unbiased!monoidal category!underlying multicategory}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be a locally small unbiased weak monoidal category.
The \textbf{underlying multicategory} $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'$ of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ has
\begin{itemize}
\item objects: objects of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$;
\item arrows: $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'(a_1, \dots, a_n; b) = \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(a_1\otimes\dots\otimes a_n, b)$;
\item composition given as follows: if $f_i \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'(a_1^i, \dots, a_{k_i}^i ;
b_i)$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$ and $g \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'(b_1, \dots, b_n; c)$, then we define
$g \circ (f_1, \dots, f_n)$ as
\[
\xymatrixnocompile{
\bigotimes_{i,j} a^i_j \ar[dd]_{f \circ (g_1, \dots, g_n)}
\ar[rr]^{\gamma \otimes \dots \otimes \gamma}
&& \bigotimes_i ( \bigotimes_j a^i_j ) \ar[dd]^{\bigotimes_i {f_i}} \\
\\
c
&& \bigotimes_i b_i \ar[ll]^g
}
\]
\end{itemize}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- defn-30: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a plain multicategory}
Let $M$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be plain multicategories.
An \textbf{algebra} for $M$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is a morphism of multicategories $M \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end defn-30 -->
<!-- defn-31: body_md -->
Let $M$ be a plain multicategory, and \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ be an unbiased monoidal category.
An \textbf{algebra} for $M$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is a morphism of multicategories from $M$
to the underlying multicategory of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end defn-31 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\index{operad!plain!concrete description}
\label{lem:operad_description}
An operad $P$ can be given by the following data:
\begin{itemize}
\item A sequence $P_0, P_1, \dots$ of sets 
\item For all $n, k_1, \dots, k_n \in \natural$, a function $\circ: P_n
\times P_{k_1} \times \dots \times P_{k_n} \to P_{\sum k_i}$ 
\item An \textbf{identity element} $1 \in P_1$
\end{itemize}
satisfying the following axioms:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Associativity:} $f \circ (g_\bullet \circ h_\bullet^\bullet) = (f \circ g_\bullet)
\circ h_\bullet^\bullet$ wherever this makes sense
\item \emph{Units:} $1 \circ f = f = f \circ (1, \dots, 1)$ for all f.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Using the symbol $*$ for the unique object, let $P_n = P(*, \dots, * ; *)$,
where the input is repeated $n$ times.
The rest of the conditions follow trivially from the definition of
a multicategory.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
Let $P$ and $Q$ be operads.
A morphism $f: P \to Q$ consists of a function $f_n : P_n \to Q_n$ for each $n
\in \natural$ such that, for all $n, k_1, \dots, k_n$, the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
P_n \times P_{k_1} \times \dots \times P_{k_n} \ar[d]_{f_n \times f_{k_1} \times \dots \times f_{k_n}} \ar[rr]^\circ
&& P_{\sum k_i} \ar[d]^{f_{\sum k_i}} \\
Q_n \times Q_{k_1} \times \dots \times Q_{k_n} \ar[rr]_\circ
&& Q_{\sum k_i}
}
\]
commutes, and that $f_1$ preserves the identity object.

If $f$ and $g$ are morphisms of operads from $P$ to $Q$, then a transformation
from $f$ to $g$ is an element $\alpha \in Q_1$ such that $\alpha \circ F p = G p \circ (\alpha, \dots, \alpha)$ for all $n \in \natural$ and all $p \in P_n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Trivial.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- defn-32: body_md -->
If a morphism of operads $f: P \to Q$ is such that $f_n$ has some property $X$
for all $n \in \natural$, we say that $f$ is \textbf{levelwise} $X$.
<!-- end defn-32 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:plEnd}
\index{endomorphism operad!plain}
Let $A$ be an object of a multicategory $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
The \textbf{endomorphism operad} of $A$ is the full sub-multicategory
$\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ whose only object is $A$.
In terms of the description in Lemma \ref{lem:operad_description}, $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n$
is the set of $n$-ary\ arrows from $A, \dots, A$ to $A$.
Composition is as in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.

In particular, if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is the underlying multicategory of some monoidal
category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'$, then $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n = \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}'(A \otimes \dots \otimes A, A)$.
This is the case we shall use most frequently.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:symmopd}
\index{\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}!as a plain operad}
\index{operad of symmetries|see{\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}}}
There is an operad $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}$ for which each $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}_n$ is the symmetric group
$S_n$.
Operadic composition is given as follows: if $\sigma \in S_n$, and $\tau_i \in
S_{k_i}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, then
\[
\sigma\circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n) : \sum_{i = 1}^j k_i + m \mapsto 
\sum_{i: \sigma(i) < \sigma(j+1)} k_i + \tau_{j+1}(m)
\]
for all $j \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $m \in \{0, \dots, k_{j+1}-1\}$.
Informally, the inputs are divided into ``blocks'' of length $k_1, k_2, \dots,
k_n$, which are then permuted by $\sigma$: the elements of each block are then
permuted by the appropriate $\tau_i$.
For an example, see Figure \ref{fig:symm_comp}.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centerline{
	\epsfxsize=5in
	               
	\epsfbox{symmcomp.eps}
}
\caption{Composition in the operad $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}$ of symmetries}
\label{fig:symm_comp}
\end{figure}
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\index{\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}}
\index{operad of braids|see{\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}}}
There is an operad $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}$ for which each $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}_n$ is the Artin braid group
$B_n$.
Composition is analogous to that for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}$: the inputs are divided into
blocks, which are braided, and then the elements of the blocks are braided.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\index{little $m$-discs operad}
\index{operad!little $m$-discs|see{little $m$-discs operad}}
Fix an $m \in \natural$.
There is an operad $LD$ for which each $LD_n$ is an embedding of $n$ copies of
the closed unit disc $D_m$ into $D_m$.
Composition is by gluing -- see Figure \ref{fig:little_discs}.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centerline{
	\epsfxsize=5in
	               
	\epsfbox{little_discs.eps}
}
\caption{Composition in the little 2-discs operad}
\label{fig:little_discs}
\end{figure}

$LD$ is known as the \textbf{little $m$-discs operad}.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- defn-33: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a plain operad}
Let $P$ be an operad.
An \textbf{algebra} for $P$ in a multicategory $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is an object $A \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$
and a morphism of operads $(\hat{\phantom{\alpha}}) : P \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$.
<!-- end defn-33 -->
<!-- defn-34: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of algebras for a plain operad}
Let $P$ be a plain operad, and $(A, (\hat{\phantom{\alpha}}))$ and $(B, (\check{\phantom{\alpha}}))$ be
algebras for $P$ in a multicategory $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
A \textbf{morphism} of algebras is an arrow $F : A \to B$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ such that,
for all $n \in \natural$, the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
	P_n \ar[d]_{(\hat{\phantom{\alpha}})} \ar[r]^{(\check{\phantom{\alpha}})}
	& \mathop{\rm{End}}(B)_n \ar[d]^{-\circ(F,\dots,F)} \\
	\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n \ar[r]^-{F\circ -} & \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A, \dots, A ; B)
}
\]
commutes.
<!-- end defn-34 -->
<!-- defn-35: body_md -->
\label{def:symm_mcat}
\index{multicategory!symmetric}
A \textbf{symmetric multicategory} is a multicategory \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ and, for every $n
\in \natural$, every $\sigma \in S_n$, and every $A_1, \dots A_n, B \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, a
map
\[
\begin{array}{rccl}
\sigma \cdot - : & \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A_1, \dots, A_n; B) & \longrightarrow 
& \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A_{\sigma 1}, \dots, A_{\sigma n}; B) \\
& f & \longmapsto & \sigma \cdot f 
\end{array}
\]
such that
\begin{itemize}
\item For each $f \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A_1, \dots, A_n; B)$, $1\cdot f = f$.
\item For each $\sigma, \rho \in S_n$, and each $f \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A_1, \dots, A_n; B)$,
\[
\rho \cdot (\sigma \cdot f) = (\rho\sigma) \cdot f
\]
\item For each permutation $\sigma \in S_n$, all objects $A^1_1, \dots,
A^n_{k_n}, B_1, \dots, B_n, C \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ and all arrows $f_i \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A^i_1, \dots,
A^i_{k_i}; B_i)$ and $g \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(B_1, \dots, B_n; C)$,
\[
(\sigma\cdot g) \circ (f_{\sigma 1}, \dots, f_{\sigma n})
	= (\sigma \circ (1,\dots, 1)) \cdot (g \circ (f_1, \dots f_n)).
\]
\item For each $A^1_1, \dots, A^n_{k_n}, B_1, \dots, B_n, C \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$,
$\sigma_i \in S_{k_i}$ for $i=1,\dots, n$, and each $f_i \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A^i_1, \dots,
A^i_{k_i}; B_i), g \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(B_1, \dots, B_n; C)$,
\[
g \circ (\sigma_1 \cdot f_1, \dots, \sigma_n \cdot f_n)
= (1 \circ (\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n)) \cdot (g\circ (f_1, \dots, f_n)).
\]
\end{itemize}
where $\sigma\circ(1, \dots, 1)$ and $1\circ(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n)$ are
as defined in Example \ref{ex:symmopd}.
<!-- end defn-35 -->
<!-- defn-36: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of symmetric multicategories}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_1$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_2$ be symmetric multicategories.
A \textbf{morphism} (or \textbf{map}) $F$ of symmetric multicategories is a
map $F: \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_1 \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_2$ of multicategories such that $F(\sigma \cdot f) = \sigma
\cdot F(f)$ for all $n \in \natural$, all $n$-ary\ $f$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}_1$, and all $\sigma
\in S_n$.
<!-- end defn-36 -->
<!-- defn-37: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a symmetric multicategory}
Let $M$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be symmetric multicategories.
An \textbf{algebra} for $M$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is a morphism of symmetric multicategories
$M \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end defn-37 -->
<!-- defn-38: body_md -->
\index{operad!symmetric}
A \textbf{symmetric operad} is a symmetric multicategory
with only one object.
<!-- end defn-38 -->
<!-- defn-39: body_md -->
\label{def:symmopd}
\xymatrixrowsep{5pc}
\xymatrixcolsep{6pc}
A \textbf{symmetric operad} is an operad $P$ together with an action of the
symmetric group $S_n$ on each $P_n$, which is compatible with the operadic
composition:
\[
\xymatrixrowsep{2pc}
\xymatrix{
	P_n \times \prod P_{k_i} \ar[r]^{(\sigma \cdot -) \times 1 \times \dots
		\times 1}
		\ar[d]_{1 \times \sigma_*} 
	& P_n \times \prod P_{k_i} \ar[dd]^{\circ} \\
	P_n \times \prod P_{\sigma k_i} \ar[d]_\circ
	\\
	P_{\sum k_i} \ar[r]^{(\sigma \circ (1, \dots, 1)) \cdot -}
	& P_{\sum k_i}
}
\xymatrix{
	P_n \times \prod P_{k_i}
		\ar[r]^{1 \times (\rho_1 \cdot -) \times \dots
			  \times (\rho_n \cdot -)}
		\ar[dd]_{\circ}
	& P_n \times \prod P_{k_i} \ar[dd]^{\circ} \\
	\\
	P_{\sum k_i} \ar[r]^{(1 \circ (\rho_1, \dots, \rho_n)) \cdot -}
	& P_{\sum k_i}
}
\]
\[
\xymatrix{
	P_n \ar@/u0.5cm/[r]^{1 \cdot -} \ar@/d0.5cm/[r]_1 & P_n
}
\]
<!-- end defn-39 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\index{\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}!as a symmetric operad}
The operad $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}$ of symmetric groups, as given in Example \ref{ex:symmopd}.
The action of $S_n$ on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}_n$ is given by $\sigma \cdot \tau = \tau\sigma^{-1}$.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:symmEnd}
\index{endomorphism operad!symmetric}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be a symmetric multicategory, and $A \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
The \textbf{symmetric endomorphism operad} $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$ of $A$ is the full sub-(symmetric multicategory) of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ whose only object is $A$.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- defn-40: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a symmetric operad}
\index{morphism!of algebras for a symmetric operad}
Let $P$ be a symmetric operad.
An \textbf{algebra} for $P$ in a multicategory $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is an object $A$ and a map $h : P \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$ of symmetric operads.
A \textbf{morphism} $(A, h) \to (A', h')$ of $P$-algebras is an arrow $F: A
\to B$ in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ such that $h'F = Fh$.
<!-- end defn-40 -->
<!-- defn-41: body_md -->
\index{multicategory!finite product}
\label{dopdef}
A \textbf{finite product multicategory} is:
\begin{itemize}
\item A plain multicategory \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}};
\item for every morphism $f : {\underline{n}} \to {\underline{m}}$ in \ensuremath{\bbF}, and for all objects $C_1,
\dots, C_n, D \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, a function $f\cdot - : \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(C_1, \dots, C_n;D) \to
\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(C_{f(1)}, \dots, C_{f(n)}; D)$
\end{itemize}
satisfying the following axioms:
\begin{itemize}
\item the \ensuremath{\bbF}-action is functorial: $f\cdot(g\cdot p) = (f\circ g)\cdot p$, and
${\rm id}_{{\underline{n}}}\cdot p = p$ wherever these equations make sense;
\item the \ensuremath{\bbF}-action and multicategorical composition interact by ``combing
out'':
\[
(f\cdot p)\circ(f_1\cdot p_1, \dots, f_n\cdot p_n) = (f\circ(f_1,\dots, f_n)) \cdot
(p\circ(p_{f(1)},\dots, p_{f(n)}))
\]
where $(f\circ(f_1,\dots, f_n))$ is given as follows:

Let $f:{\underline{n}} \to {\underline{m}}$, and $f_i:{{\underline{k}}}_i \to {{\underline{j}}_i}$ for $i = 1, \dots,
n$.
Then
\[
\begin{array}{rcccl}
f\circ(f_1, \dots, f_n) & : & {\underline{\sum k_i}} & \to & {\underline{\sum j_i}} \\
f\circ(f_1,\dots, f_n) & : & \left(\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} k_{f(i)}\right) + h
	& \mapsto & \left(\sum_{i=1}^{f(p)-1} j_i\right) + f_p(h)
\end{array}
\]
for all $p \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and all $h \in \{1, \dots, k_{f(p)}\}$.
See Figure \ref{combfig}.
The small specks represent inputs to the arrow that are ignored.
\end{itemize}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centerline{
                
	\epsfysize=2in
	\epsfbox{combing.eps}
}
\caption{``Combing out'' the \ensuremath{\bbF}-action}
\label{combfig}
\end{figure}
<!-- end defn-41 -->
<!-- defn-42: body_md -->
\index{operad!finite product}
A \textbf{finite product operad} is a finite product multicategory\ with only one object.
<!-- end defn-42 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a ring}
\label{ex:Ralg_fp}
Let $R$ be a ring, and $P_n = R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ (the set of polynomials in
$n$ commuting variables over $R$) for all $n \in \natural$.
If $p \in P_n$ and $q_i \in P_{k_i}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, then
\[
(p\circ(q_1, \dots, q_n))(x_1, \dots, x_{\sum_{i=1}^n k_i}) =
	p(q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{k_1}), \dots, q_n(x_{(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i) + 1},
		\dots, x_{\sum_{i=1}^n k_i}))
\]
and if $f: {\underline{n}} \to {\underline{m}}$, then
\[
(f \cdot p)(x_1, \dots, x_m) = p(x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(n)})
\]
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\index{commutative monoids}
\label{ex:comm_monoid_fp}
Let $P_n$ be the set of elements of the free commutative monoid on $n$
variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$.
Elements of $P_n$ are in one-to-one-correspondence with  elements of
$\natural^n$.
We call the $n$th component of $p \in P_n$ the \textbf{multiplicity of the
$n$th argument}.
Composition is defined as follows:
\def\left[\begin{array}{c} {#} \\ \vdots \\ {1}\end{array}\right]#2{\left[\begin{array}{c} {#1} \\ \vdots \\ {#2}\end{array}\right]}
\def\left[\begin{array}{c} {#_1} \\ \vdots \\ {#_{1}}\end{array}\right]#2{\left[\begin{array}{c} {#1_1} \\ \vdots \\ {#1_1_{#2}}\end{array}\right]}
\[
\left[\begin{array}{c} {p_1} \\ \vdots \\ {p_{n}}\end{array}\right] \circ \left(\left[\begin{array}{c} {q^1_1} \\ \vdots \\ {q^1_{k_1}}\end{array}\right], \dots, \left[\begin{array}{c} {q^n_1} \\ \vdots \\ {q^n_{k_n}}\end{array}\right]\right)
= \left[\begin{array}{c} {p_1 q_1^1} \\ \vdots \\ {p_n q^n_{k_n}}\end{array}\right]
\]
and if $f : {\underline{n}} \to {\underline{m}}$,
\[
f \cdot \left[\begin{array}{c} {p_1} \\ \vdots \\ {p_{n}}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{c} {\sum_{f(i)=1} p_i} \\ \vdots \\ {\sum_{f(i)=m} p_i}\end{array}\right]
\]
Or, in more familiar notation:
\begin{eqnarray*}
(x_1^{p_1} \dots x_n^{p_n}) \circ (x_1^{q^1_1} \dots x_1^{q^1_{k_1}}, \dots
x_{(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i) + 1}^{q^n_1} \dots x_{\sum_{i=1}^n k_i}^{q^n_{k_n}})
& = &x_1^{p_1 q^1_1} x_2^{p_1 q^1_1} \dots x_{\sum_{i=1}^n k_i}^{p_n q^n_{k_n}}
\\
f\cdot(x_1^{p_1} \dots x_n^{p_n}) & = & x_{f(1)}^{p_1} \dots x_{f(n)}^{p_n} \\
 & = & x_1^{\sum_{f(i)=1} p_i} \dots x_m^{\sum_{f(i)=m} p_i}
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{ex:fpEnd}
\index{endomorphism operad!finite product}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be a finite product category, and $A$ be an object of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Then there is a finite product operad\ $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$, the \textbf{endomorphism operad} of $A$,
where $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)_n = \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}(A^n,A)$, and $f\cdot p$ is $p$ composed with the
appropriate combination of projections to relabel its arguments by $f$.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- defn-43: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of finite product multicategories}
Let $M$, $N$ be finite product multicategories.
A \textbf{morphism} $F: M \to N$ consists of
\begin{itemize}
\item for each object $m \in M$, an object $Fm \in N$;
\item for each $n \in \natural$ and all $m_1, \dots, m_n, m \in M$, a map
\[
F_{m_1, \dots, m_n, m}: M(m_1, \dots m_n; m) \to N(Fm_1, \dots, Fm_n; Fm)
\]
commuting with the \ensuremath{\bbF}-action, the unit and composition.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-43 -->
<!-- defn-44: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a finite product multicategory}
Let $M$ be a finite product multicategory.
An \textbf{algebra} for $M$ in a finite product multicategory\ $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is a map of finite product multicategories\ $M \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
An \textbf{algebra} for $M$ in a finite product category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is a map of
finite product multicategories\ from $M$ to the underlying finite product multicategory\ of \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}.
Finite product multicategories\ and their morphisms form a category called {\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Multicat}}}}}. \index{{\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}}}
<!-- end defn-44 -->
<!-- defn-45: body_md -->
\index{morphism!of finite product operads}
Let $P$, $Q$ be finite product operads.
A \textbf{morphism} $F: P \to Q$ is a sequence of maps $F_i: P_i \to
Q_i$ commuting with the \ensuremath{\bbF}\ action, the unit and composition.
<!-- end defn-45 -->
<!-- defn-46: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a finite product operad}
Let $P$ be a finite product operad.
An \textbf{algebra} for $P$ in a finite product category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ is an object $A
\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ and a map of finite product operads\ $P \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$.
<!-- end defn-46 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\index{algebra!for a ring}
The algebras in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ for the operad described in Example \ref{ex:Ralg_fp} are
associative $R$-algebras in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
\index{commutative monoids}
The algebras for the operad described in Example \ref{ex:comm_monoid_fp} are
commutative monoid objects in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:DOpCat iso Clone}
${\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}} \cong \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Clone}}}}$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We shall construct a functor $K_{(-)} : {\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}} \to \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Clone}}}}$, and show that it is
bijective on objects, full and faithful.

If $P$ is a finite product operad, let $K_P$ be the following clone:
\begin{itemize}
\item $(K_P)_n = P_n$ for all $n \in \natural$,
\item composition is given by composition in $P$: if $p \in P_n$ and $p_1,
\dots, p_n \in P_m$, then $p\bullet(p_1, \dots, p_n) \in (K_P)_m$ is $f \cdot
(p\circ(p_1, \dots, p_n)) \in P_m$, where
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:KPcomp}
\begin{array}{lccl}
f : &{\underline{nm}} &\to & {\underline{m}} \\
& x & \mapsto & ((x - 1) \mod m) + 1,
\end{array}
\end{equation}
\item for all $n \in \natural$ and all $i \in {\underline{n}}$, the projection
$\delta^i_n$ is $f^i_n \cdot 1$, where
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:KPproj}
\begin{array}{lccl}
f^i_n : &{\underline{1}} &\to & {\underline{n}} \\
& 1 & \mapsto & i.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
It is easily checked that $K_P$ satisfies the axioms for a clone given in
Definition \ref{def:clone}.

On morphisms, $K_{(-)}$ acts trivially: morphisms of clones and of finite product operads\ are
simply maps of signatures commuting with the extra structure, and $K_{(-)}$
preserves the underlying map of signatures.

Let $K$ be a clone.
Let $P_K$ be the finite product operad\ for which
\begin{itemize}
\item $(P_K)_n = K_n$ for all $n \in \natural$,
\item $1 = \delta^1_1$,
\item $p \circ (p_1, \dots, p_n) = p \bullet (p_1 \bullet (\delta^1_m, \dots,
\delta^{k_1}_{\sum k_i}), \dots, p_n \bullet (\delta^{k_1 + \dots + k_{n-1} +
1}_{\sum k_i}, \dots, \delta^{\sum k_i}_{\sum k_i}))$ for all $n$ and $k_1,
\dots, k_n \in \natural$, all $p \in K_n$, and all $p_1 \in K_{k_1}, \dots, p_n
\in K_{k_n}$,
\item $f \cdot p = p \bullet (\delta^{f(1)}_m, \dots, \delta^{f(n)}_m)$ for all
$n, m \in \natural$, all $f : {\underline{n}} \to {\underline{m}}$ and all $p \in K_n$.
\end{itemize}
We will show that $K_{P_K} = K$ for all $K \in \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Clone}}}}$, and that $P_{K_P} = P$
for all $P \in {\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}}$.
Let $K$ be a clone.
Then $(K_{P_K})_n = (P_K)_n = K_n$ for all $n \in \natural$.
If $n, m \in \natural$, $k \in K_n$ and $k_1, \dots, k_n \in K_m$, then the
composite $k\bullet(k_1, \dots, k_n)$ in $K_{P_K}$ is given by the composite 
$f \cdot (k\circ(k_1, \dots, k_n))$ in $P_K$, where $f$ is given by
(\ref{eqn:KPcomp}) above.
This in turn is given by the composite
\begin{eqnarray*}
(k & \bullet & (k_1 \bullet (\delta^1_{nm},
\dots, \delta^{m}_{nm}), \dots, k_n \bullet (\delta^{(n-1)m + 1}_{nm}, \dots,
\delta^{nm}_{nm}))) \\
& \bullet & (\delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m, \dots, \delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m)
\end{eqnarray*}
in $K$.
By the associativity law for clones, this is equal to
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
k \bullet (& k_1 \bullet (\delta^1_{nm}, \dots, \delta^{m}_{nm})
 \bullet (\delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m, \dots, \delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m), \\
& \dots, \\
& k_n \bullet (\delta^{(n-1)m + 1}_{nm}, \dots,\delta^{nm}_{nm}) 
 \bullet (\delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m, \dots, \delta^1_m, \dots, \delta^m_m))
\end{array}
\]
which in turn may be simplified to $k \bullet (k_1, \dots, k_n)$ as required.
For every $n \in \natural$ and every $i \in {\underline{n}}$, the projection
$\delta^i_n$ in $K_{P_K}$ is given by $f^i_n \cdot 1$, where $f^i_n$ is defined
in (\ref{eqn:KPproj}): this in turn is given by $1 \circ
(\delta^i_n) = \delta^1_1 \bullet (\delta^i_n) = \delta^i_n$.
Hence $K_{P_K} = K$.

Conversely, let $P$ be a finite product operad\; we shall show that $P_{K_P} = P$.
For every $n \in \natural$, the set $(P_{K_P})_n$ is equal to $P_n$.
The unit element is given by $1 = \delta^1_1 = f^1_1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
If $p \in P_n$ and $p_i \in P_{k_i}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, then the composite
$p\circ(p_1, \dots, p_n)$ is given by $p \bullet (p_1 \bullet (\delta^1_m, \dots,
\delta^{k_1}_{\sum k_i}), \dots, p_n \bullet (\delta^{k_1 + \dots + k_{n-1} +
1}_{\sum k_i}, \dots, \delta^{\sum k_i}_{\sum k_i}))$ in $K_P$, which in turn
is given by (after simplification) $p \circ (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in $P$.
Hence $P = P_{K_P}$, and $K_{(-)}$ is bijective on objects.
The reasoning above also suffices to show that $K_{(-)}$ is well-defined on
morphisms and full (since preserving a finite product operad\ structure amounts exactly to
preserving the associated clone structure).
Since the morphisms of both categories are simply maps of signatures with extra
properties and $K_{(-)}$ commutes with the forgetful functors to
$\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}^\natural$,
then $K_{(-)}$ is faithful.
Hence $K_{(-)}$ is an isomorphism of categories, and ${\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}} \cong \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Clone}}}}$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:dop-clone alg}
Let $P$ be a finite product operad.
Then $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(P)$}}}} \cong \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(K_P)$}}}}$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $(A, (\hat{\phantom{\alpha}}))$ be a $P$-algebra.
Since the elements of the finite product endomorphism operad $\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$ are
endomorphisms of $A$, and composition is given by composition of morphisms,
then $K_{\mathop{\rm{End}}(A)} = \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$, the endomorphism clone of $A$.
Since the functor $K_{(-)} : {\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP-Operad}}}}} \to \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Clone}}}}$ is an isomorphism, a morphism
of finite product operads\ $P \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$ is exactly a map of clones $K_P \to \mathop{\rm{End}}(A)$.
Hence an algebra for $P$ is exactly an algebra for $K_P$.
A morphism between $P$-algebras is a morphism between their underlying objects
that commutes with $\hat p$ for every $p \in P_n$ and every $n \in \natural$;
this is true iff it commutes with $\hat k$ for every $k \in (K_P)_n$ and every
$n \in \natural$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:frees_exist}
Let $\Csmall$ and $\Dsmall$ be small finite-product categories, let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be
cartesian closed and have all small colimits, and let $Q: \Csmall \to \Dsmall$
preserve finite products.
Then the adjunction
\[
                           
	\xymatrix{
		[\Dsmall,\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}] \ar@<1ex>[r]^-{Q_!}_-{\bot}
		& [\Csmall,\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}] \ar@<1.1ex>[l]^-{Q^*}
	}
,
\]
where $Q^*$ is composition with $Q$ and $Q_! = \mathop{\rm{Lan}}_Q$, restricts to an
adjunction
\[
                           
	\xymatrix{
		\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Dsmall,\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \ar@<1ex>[r]^-{Q_!}_-{\bot}
		& \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Csmall,\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \ar@<1.1ex>[l]^-{Q^*}
	}
,
\]
\label{lem:leftadj}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
\def[\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]{[\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]}
\def[\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]{[\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]}
\def\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}){\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})}
\def\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}){\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})}
Certainly $Q^*$ restricts in this way, since $Q$ preserves finite products.
$\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})$ and $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})$ are full subcategories of $[\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]$
and $[\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}]$, so if we can show that $Q_!$ restricts to a functor $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Csmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \to
\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{FP}}}}(\Dsmall, \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})$, then it is automatically left adjoint to the restriction of $Q^*$.

Let $X : \Csmall \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ preserve finite products.
We must show that $Q_! X : \Dsmall \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ preserves finite products.
We shall proceed by showing that $Q_! X$ preserves terminal objects and binary
products.

Recall that
\[
(Q_! X)(b) \cong \int^a \Dsmall(Q a, b) \times X a
\]
for all $b \in \Dsmall$.
Hence, using $1$ for the terminal objects in $\Dsmall$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
(Q_! X)(1) & \cong & \int^a \Dsmall(Q a, 1) \times X a \\
& \cong & \int^a 1 \times X a \\
& \cong & \int^a X a \\
& \cong & X 1 \\
& \cong & 1
\end{eqnarray*}
since $X$ preserves finite products and the colimit of a diagram $D$ over a
category with a terminal object $1$ is simply $D 1$.

Now, let $b_1, b_2 \in \Dsmall$.
Then
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:defQ!}
\nonumber\lefteqn{(Q_! X)(b_1 \times b_2)} \\
& \cong & \int^a \Dsmall(Q a, b_1 \times b_2) \times X a
\\
\label{eq:defprod1}
& \cong & \int^a \Dsmall(Q a, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q a, b_2) \times X a \\
\label{eq:density1}
& \cong & \int^a
	\left(\int^{c_1} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Csmall(a, c_1) \right)
	\times
	\left(\int^{c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times \Csmall(a, c_2) \right)
	\times Xc \\
\label{eq:dist1}
& \cong & \int^{a, c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times
	\Csmall(a, c_1) \times \Csmall(a, c_2) \times X a \\
\label{eq:defprod2}
& \cong & \int^{a, c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times
	\Csmall(a, c_1 \times c_2) \times X a \\
\label{eq:dist2}
& \cong & \int^{c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times
	\left( \int^a \Csmall(a, c_1 \times c_2) \times X a \right) \\
\label{eq:density2}
& \cong & \int^{c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times
	X(c_1 \times c_2) \\
\label{eq:defprod3}
& \cong & \int^{c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times
	X c_1 \times X c_2 \\
\label{eq:Xprod}
& \cong & \int^{c_1, c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times X c_1 \times
	\Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times X c_2 \\
\label{eq:rearrange}
& \cong & \left (\int^{c_1} \Dsmall(Q c_1, b_1) \times X c_1 \right) \times
	\left( \int^{c_2} \Dsmall(Q c_2, b_2) \times X c_2 \right) \\
\label{eq:dist3}
& \cong & (Q_!X)(b_1) \times (Q_!X)(b_2)
\end{eqnarray}
(\ref{eq:defQ!}) is the definition of $Q_!$;
(\ref{eq:defprod1}), (\ref{eq:defprod2}) and (\ref{eq:defprod3}) are from the
definition of products;
(\ref{eq:density1}) and (\ref{eq:density2}) are applications of the Density
Formula;
(\ref{eq:dist1}), (\ref{eq:dist2}) and (\ref{eq:dist3}) use the
distributivity of products over colimits in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ (since \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\ is cartesian
closed),
and (\ref{eq:Xprod}) uses the fact that $X$ preserves finite products.

So $Q_!$ preserves terminal objects and binary products, and hence all finite
products.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
The functors ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\Sigma}}}, {\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\rm pl}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}}}$ all have left adjoints.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:monadj}
Let $S$ be a set, whose elements we will call \textbf{sorts}.
Let $T$ and $T'$ be $S$-sorted finite product theories, such that $T'$ is a
subcategory of $T$ and the inclusion of $T'$ into $T$ preserves finite
products.
Let $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T)$}}}}$ be the category of $T$-algebras and morphisms in some finite
product category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T')$}}}}$ be the category of $T'$-algebras and
morphisms in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Then the free/forgetful adjunction
\[ 
                           
	\xymatrix{
		\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T')$}}}} \ar@<1ex>[r]^-{F}_-{\bot}
		& \ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T)$}}}} \ar@<1.1ex>[l]^-{U}
	}

\]
is monadic, provided the left adjoint $F$ exists.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
\def\prod # s_i1{\prod #1 s_i}
\def\prod # r_j1{\prod #1 r_j}
\def\prod #_{s_i}1{\prod #1_{s_i}}
\def\prod #_{r_j}1{\prod #1_{r_j}}
We will make use of Beck's theorem to prove monadicity: precisely, we shall
make use of the version in \cite{catwork} VI.7.1, which states that $U$ is
monadic if it has a left adjoint and it strictly creates coequalizers for
$U$-absolute coequalizer pairs.
Recall that a functor $G: \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}} \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}$ \textbf{strictly creates coequalizers}
for a diagram $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ if, for every coequalizer $e: GB
\to E$ of $Gf$ and $Gg$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}$, there are a unique object $E'$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ and a
unique arrow $e' : B \to E'$ such that $GE' = E$ and $Ge' = e$, and moreover
that $e'$ is a coequalizer of $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $.

Let $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $ be a $U$-absolute coequalizer pair in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T)$}}}}$,
and $e: U B \to E$ be the coequalizer of $ \xymatrix{UA \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{Uf} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{Ug} & UB} $.
We wish to extend $E$ to a functor $E': T \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Define $E'$ to be equal to $E$ on objects.
On arrows, we shall define $E'$ using the universal property of $E$ and the
$U$-absolute property of $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $.

For each arrow $\phi : s_1 \times \dots \times s_n \to r_1 \times \dots
\times r_m$ in $T$ (where $s_i, r_j \in S$),
consider the diagram
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:coeq}
\xymatrixrowsep{4pc}
\xymatrixcolsep{4pc}
\xymatrixnocompile{
	\prod U A s_i \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\prod U f_{s_i}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\prod Ug_{s_i}} \ar[d]_{A\phi}
	& \prod U B s_i \ar[r]^{\prod e_{s_i}} \ar[d]_{B\phi}
	& \prod E s_i \ar@{..>}[d]^{E'\phi}\\
	\prod U A r_j \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\prod f_{r_j}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\prod g_{r_j}}
	& \prod U B r_j \ar[r]^{\prod e_{r_j}}
	& \prod E r_j
}
\end{equation}
in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$, where $e: UB \to E$ is a coequalizer for $ \xymatrix{UA \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{Uf} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{Ug} & UB} $.

Since $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $ is a $U$-absolute coequalizer pair, $\prod e_{s_i}
: \prod UB s_i \to \prod E s_i$ is a coequalizer.
Since $f$ and $g$ are $T$-homomorphisms, (\ref{eqn:coeq}) serially commutes, so
$(\prod e_{r_j})\phi$ factors uniquely through $\prod e_{s_i}$.
Define $E'\phi$ to be this map, as shown (and note that $E'\phi = E\phi$ if
$\phi$ is in $T'$).
This definition straightforwardly makes $E'$ into a functor $T \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Since $E$ is a $T'$-algebra, and products in $T$ are the same as products in
$T'$, we may deduce that $E': T\to C$ preserves finite products, and thus is
a $T$-algebra.
Clearly, $E'$ is the unique extension of $E$ to a $T$-algebra such that $e$ is
a $T$-algebra morphism.
It remains to show that $e$ is a coequalizer map for $ \xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B} $ in
$\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T)$}}}}$.

Suppose $
	\xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B \ar[r]^-{d} & D }
$ is a fork in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T)$}}}}$.
Then $
	\xymatrix{UA \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{Uf} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{Ug} & UB \ar[r]^-{Ud} & UD }
$ is a fork in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Alg$(T')$}}}}$, so $Ud$
factors through $e$; say $Ud = he$.
We must show that $h$ is a $T$-homomorphism.
As before, take $\phi : s_1 \times \dots \times s_n \to r_1 \times \dots \times
r_m$ in $T$, and consider the diagram
\begin{equation}
\xymatrixcolsep{4pc}
\xymatrixnocompile{
	\prod U A s_i \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\prod U f_{s_i}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\prod U g_{s_i}} \ar[dd]_{A\phi}
	& \prod U B s_i \ar[r]^{\prod e_{s_i}}
		\ar[dd]_{B\phi} \ar[dr]_{\prod Ud_{s_i}}
	& \prod E' s_i \ar@/r1cm/[dd]^{E'\phi} \ar@{..>}[d]_{\prod h_{s_i}} \\
	& & \prod U D s_i \ar@/r1cm/[dd]^{D\phi} \\
	\prod U A r_j \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\prod f_{r_j}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\prod g_{r_j}}
	& \prod U B r_j \ar[r]^{\prod e_{r_j}} \ar[dr]_{\prod Ud_{r_j}}
	& \prod E' r_j \ar@{..>}[d]_{\prod h_{r_j}} \\
	& & \prod D r_j
}
\end{equation}

We must show that the curved square on the far right commutes.
Now $(D\phi) \circ (\prod d_{s_i}) = (D\phi) \circ (\prod h_{s_i}) \circ (\prod e_{s_i})$, and $(\prod Ud_{r_j})\circ(UB\phi) = h\circ e\circ(UB\phi) = h \circ
(E\phi) \circ (\prod e_{s_i})$, since $e$ is a $T$-algebra homomorphism.
But $(\prod Ud_{r_j})\circ \phi = \phi \circ (\prod d_i)$, so $D\phi \circ
(\prod h_{s_i}) \circ (\prod e_{s_i}) = h \circ (E\phi) \circ (\prod e_{s_i})$.
And $\prod e_{s_i}$ is (regular) epic, so $h \circ (E\phi) = (D\phi) \circ
(\prod h_{s_i})$.

So $h$ is a $T$-algebra homomorphism.
Hence $U$ strictly creates coequalizers for $U$-absolute coequalizer pairs,
and hence is monadic.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:opd monadic over setN}
\index{\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Operad}}}}!monadicity over $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}^\natural$}
All the adjunctions in diagram \ref{eqn:adjs}, namely ${\ensuremath{F_{\rm fp}^{\Sigma}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\Sigma}}}, {\ensuremath{F_{\rm fp}^{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\rm pl}}}, {\ensuremath{F_{\rm fp}}} \dashv
{\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}}}, {\ensuremath{F_{\Sigma}^{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}, {\ensuremath{F_{\Sigma}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$, are
monadic.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Each category mentioned is a category of algebras for some $\natural$-sorted
theory, and the monadicity of each adjunction mentioned is obtained by a simple
application of Lemma \ref{lem:monadj}. For instance, symmetric operads are
algebras for the theory presented by
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{operations}: one of the appropriate arity for each composition
operation in Definition \ref{def:symmopd}, and an operation $\sigma \cdot -$
for each $n \in \natural$ and each $\sigma$ in $S_n$.
\item \emph{equations}: one for each instance of the axioms in Definition
\ref{def:symmopd}, and an equation $(\sigma \cdot -)\circ (\rho \cdot -) =
\sigma\rho \cdot -$ for each $\sigma, \rho \in S_n$ and every $n \in \natural$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- defn-47: body_md -->
\label{def:srterm}
\index{tree!strongly regular}
\index{strongly regular!tree|see{tree, strongly regular}}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature.
An \textbf{$n$-ary\ strongly regular tree labelled by $\Phi$} is an element of
the set $\mathop{\mbox{tr}}_n \Phi$, which is recursively defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $|$ is an element of $\mathop{\mbox{tr}}_1 \Phi$.
\item If $\phi \in \Phi_n$, and $\tau_1 \in \mathop{\mbox{tr}}_{k_1} \Phi, \dots, \tau_n \in
\mathop{\mbox{tr}}_{k_n} \Phi$, then $\phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n) \in
\mathop{\mbox{tr}}_{\sum k_i} \Phi$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-47 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
$({\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}, {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}, \eta, \epsilon)$ is an adjunction.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We proceed by checking the triangle identities.
We require to show that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eqn:triarrFp}
\xymatrix{
	{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \ar[r]^{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}\eta} \ar[dr]_{1_{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}}}
	& {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \ar[d]^{\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}} \\
	& {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}
} \\
\label{eqn:triarrUp}
\xymatrix{
	{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \ar[r]^{\eta{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}} \ar[dr]_{1_{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}}}
	& {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \ar[d]^{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon} \\
	& {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}
}
\end{eqnarray}
commute.
For (\ref{eqn:triarrFp}), we proceed by induction on trees.
We shall suppress all subscripts on natural transformations in the interest of
legibility.
For the base case:
\begin{eqnarray*}
\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} ( {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}\eta (|)) & = & \epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} (| \circ(|)) \\
	& = & | \circ(\epsilon(|)) \\
	& = & | \\
	& = & 1_{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}(|).
\end{eqnarray*}
For the inductive step, let $\Phi$ be a signature, $\phi$ be an $n$-ary\ element of $\Phi$, and $\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n$ be trees labelled by $\Phi$.
Then:
\begin{eqnarray*}
(\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}) ( ({\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}\eta) (\phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n) ))
	& = & \epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} (\phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n)\circ(|, \dots, |)) \\
	& = & \phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n)
		\circ((\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}})(|), \dots, (\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}})(|)) \\
	& = & \phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n) \\
	& = & 1_{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}(\phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n))
\end{eqnarray*}

Hence $\epsilon{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \circ {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}\eta = 1{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}$, as required.

For (\ref{eqn:triarrUp}), let $P$ be a plain operad, and let $p$ be an $n$-ary\
arrow in $P$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon) ((\eta{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}) (p)) & = & {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon (p\circ(|, \dots, |)) \\
	& = & p\circ(({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon)(|), \dots, ({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon)(|)) \\
	& = & p\circ(1, \dots, 1) \\
	& = & p \\
	& = & 1_{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}(p)
\end{eqnarray*}
So ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}\epsilon \circ \eta{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} = 1_{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$, as required.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:Stimes=Fsigp}
$(\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -) $ is left adjoint to ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}$.
The unit of the adjunction is given by 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\eta: 1 & \to & {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} (\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -) \\
\eta_P: p & \mapsto & (1, p),
\end{eqnarray*}
and the counit is given by 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\epsilon : (\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -) {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} & \to & 1 \\
\epsilon_P : (\sigma, p) & \mapsto & \sigma \cdot p.
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
As before, we proceed by checking the triangle identities.
First, let $P$ be a plain operad, $p$ be an $n$-ary\ arrow in $P$, and $\sigma
\in S_n$.
Then $(\sigma, p)$ is an element of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times P$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
(\epsilon(\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -)) (\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times \eta) (\sigma, p))
	& = & (\epsilon(\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -)) (\sigma , (1, p)) \\
	& = & \sigma \cdot (1, p) \\
	& = & (\sigma \circ 1, p) \\
	& = & (\sigma, p)
\end{eqnarray*}

Now let $P'$ be a symmetric operad, and $p'$ be an $n$-ary\ arrow in $P'$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
({\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}\epsilon) (\eta{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}(p')) & = & ({\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}\epsilon)((1, p')) \\
	& = & 1 \cdot p' \\
	& = & p'
\end{eqnarray*}

So the triangle identities are indeed satisfied, and $(\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}} \times -)\dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- defn-48: body_md -->
\label{def:permtree}
\index{tree!permuted}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature.
An \textbf{$n$-ary\ permuted tree labelled by $\Phi$} is an element of $({\ensuremath{F_{\Sigma}^{\rm pl}}}
{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)_n = ({\ensuremath{F_{\Sigma}}} \Phi)_n$.
\index{tree!finite product}
An \textbf{$n$-ary\ finite product tree labelled by $\Phi$} is an element of
$({\ensuremath{F_{\rm fp}}} \Phi)_n$.
<!-- end defn-48 -->
<!-- defn-49: body_md -->
\label{def:sreqn}
\index{equation!plain-operadic}
Let $\Phi$ be a signature.
A \textbf{plain-operadic equation over $\Phi$ in $n$ variables} is an element
of $(({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)_n)^2$ (that is, a pair of $n$-ary\ strongly regular trees over
$\Phi$), and a \textbf{plain-operadic equation over $\Phi$} is an element of
$\sum_n (({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)_n)^2$.
<!-- end defn-49 -->
<!-- defn-50: body_md -->
\label{def:opd_presentation}
\index{presentation!for a plain operad}
Let $P$ be a plain operad.
A \textbf{presentation} for $P$ is a signature $\Phi$, a signature $E$, and
maps $e_1, e_2 : {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} E \to {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi $ such that, for some $\phi$,
\[
\NoCompileMatrices

	\xymatrix{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} E \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{e_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{e_2} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi \ar[r]^-{\phi} & P }

\]
is a coequalizer.
We say that a regular epi $\phi : {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi \to P$ \textbf{generates} $P$, or
that $\phi$ (or, where the choice of $\phi$ is clear, $\Phi$) is a
\textbf{generator} of $P$.
<!-- end defn-50 -->
<!-- defn-51: body_md -->
Let $P$ be a plain operad, and $\phi : {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi \to P$ be a generator for $P$.
Let $E$ be a subsignature of $({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)^2$, so that each $E_n$ is a set of
$n$-ary\ $\Phi$-equations. 
Let $i$ be the inclusion map $\xymatrix{E \ar@{^{((}->}[r] & ({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)^2 }$, and
$\pi_1, \pi_2$ be the projection maps $({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi)^2 \to {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi$.
Then $P$ \textbf{satisfies all equations in $E$} if the diagram
\[
\NoCompileMatrices

	\xymatrix{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} E \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\overline{\pi_1 i}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\overline{\pi_2 i}} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \Phi \ar[r]^-{\phi} & P }

\]
is a fork.
<!-- end defn-51 -->
<!-- defn-52: body_md -->
\index{kernel pair}
Let $f: A \to B$ in some category $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
The \textbf{kernel pair} of $f$ is the pair $ \xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{p} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{q} & A} $ of maps in
the pullback square
\[
\NoCompileMatrices

	\xymatrix{
		W \ar@{}[dr]|-<{\textstyle{\lrcorner}} \ar[r]^-{p} \ar[d]_-{q}
		& A \ar[d]^-{f} \\
		A \ar[r]^-{f}
		& B
	}

\]
if this pullback exists.
<!-- end defn-52 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:sreqns}
Let $\epsilon$ be the counit of the adjunction ${\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$.
Let $ \xymatrix{Q \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\pi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\pi_2} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{({\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P)}} $ be the kernel
pair of the component
\[
\epsilon_{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P} : {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P = {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P \to {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P,
\]
of $\epsilon$.
Let $h$ be the unique map $Q \to ({\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P)^2$ induced by $\pi_1, \pi_2$.
Then the image of ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} h$ is the largest signature of plain-operadic ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}}
P$-equations satisfied by $P$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
$Q, \pi_1, \pi_2$ are given by the diagram
\[
\NoCompileMatrices

	\xymatrix{
		Q \ar@{}[dr]|-<{\textstyle{\lrcorner}} \ar[r]^-{\pi_1} \ar[d]_-{\pi_2}
		& {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P \ar[d]^-{\epsilon} \\
		{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P \ar[r]^-{\epsilon}
		& {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P
	}

\]
As a right adjoint, ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$ preserves pullbacks; we take the standard
construction of pullbacks in $\ensuremath{\mbox{\upshape{\textbf{Set}}}}^\natural$ as subobjects of products, in
which case $h$ is an inclusion map.
An element of $({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} Q)_n$ is then a pair $(e_1, e_2)$ of $n$-ary\ strongly regular
${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P$ trees such that $\epsilon(e_1) = \epsilon(e_2)$.
Hence, $Q$ is a signature of plain-operadic ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P$-equations satisfied by
$P$.
Conversely, let $E$ be a signature of plain-operadic ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P$-equations
satisfied by $P$, and let $(e_1, e_2)$ be an element of $E_n$:
then $\epsilon(e_1) = \epsilon(e_2)$ and so $(e_1, e_2)$ is an element of $({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}
Q)_n$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:srpres}
Let $R$ be the plain operad generated by ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P$, satisfying exactly those
plain-operadic equations satisfied by $P$.
Then
\[
\xymatrixcolsep{4pc}
 \xymatrix{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} Q \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\overline{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \pi_{1}}} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\overline{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \pi_{2}}} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P} 
\]
is a presentation for $R$, where the overbars refer to transposition with
respect to the adjunction ${\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:mon=>regep}
The counit of a monadic adjunction is componentwise regular epi.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
See \cite{acc} 20.15.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:fork.epi}
If $
	\xymatrix{X \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & Y \ar[r]^-{h} & Z }
$ is a coequalizer in some category, and if $e: W \to X$
is epi, then $
	\xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{fe} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{ge} & Y \ar[r]^-{h} & Z }
$ is a coequalizer.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Suppose $
	\xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{fe} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{ge} & Y \ar[r]^-{i} & A }
$ is a fork.
Then $ife = ige$, so $if = ig$ since $e$ is epi.
So $
	\xymatrix{X \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & Y \ar[r]^-{i} & A }
$ is a fork, and hence $i$ factors uniquely through $h$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:coeq-kerpair}
In categories with all kernel pairs, every regular epi is the coequalizer of
its kernel pair.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ have all kernel pairs, and $
	\xymatrix{A \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{g} & B \ar[r]^-{e} & C }
$ be a coequalizer
diagram in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Let $ \xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{p} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{q} & B} $ be the kernel pair of $e$.
We will show that $
	\xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{p} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{q} & B \ar[r]^-{e} & C }
$ is a coequalizer diagram.
Since $ef = eg$, we may uniquely factor $(f,g)$ through W:
\[
\xymatrix{
A \ar[ddr]_g \ar[rrd]^f \ar@{..>}[dr]|i \\
& W \ar@{}[dr]|-<{\textstyle{\lrcorner}} \ar[r]_p \ar[d]^q
& B \ar[d]_e \\
& B \ar[r]^e
& C
}
\]
Suppose $
	\xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{p} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{q} & B \ar[r]^-{h} & D }
$ is a fork.
$hp = hq$, so $hpi = hqi$, so $hf = hg$.
By the universal property of $e$, we may factor $h$ uniquely through $e$.
So $
	\xymatrix{W \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{p} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{q} & B \ar[r]^-{e} & C }
$ is a coequalizer diagram, as required.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
Let $P$ be a symmetric operad, and let $Q, \pi_1, \pi_2$ be as in Lemma
\ref{lem:sreqns}.
Then the coequalizer of the diagram
\[
 \xymatrix{Q \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\pi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\pi_1} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P} 
\]
is ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let $\epsilon'$ be the unit of the adjunction ${\ensuremath{F_{\Sigma}^{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}$.
This adjunction is monadic, so $\epsilon_{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P}$ is regular epi by Lemma
\ref{lem:mon=>regep}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:coeq-kerpair}, $\epsilon_{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P}$ is the coequalizer of its kernel pair, i.e.
\[
\NoCompileMatrices

	\xymatrix{Q \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\pi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\pi_2} & \sum_n({\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P)_n \ar[r]^-{\epsilon_{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P}} & {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P }

\]
is a coequalizer diagram.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\index{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}}!explicit construction}
Let $P$ be a symmetric operad.
Then ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P$ is the plain operad whose operations are those in $P$,
satisfying exactly those plain-operadic equations which are true in $P$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The adjunction ${\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}} \dashv {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}}$ is monadic, so if $\epsilon'$ is its
counit, then $\epsilon'_Q : {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} Q \to Q$ is (regular) epi by Lemma
\ref{lem:mon=>regep}.
Hence, by Lemma \ref{lem:fork.epi},
\def\pi_{#} \epsilon'_Q1{\pi_{#1} \epsilon'_Q}
\[

	\xymatrix{{\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} Q \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\pi_{1} \epsilon'_Q} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\pi_{2} \epsilon'_Q} & {\ensuremath{F_{\rm pl}}}{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P \ar[r]^-{\epsilon_{{\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P}} & {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P }

\]
is a coequalizer.
But $\pi_{1} \epsilon'_Q = \overline{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \pi_1}$, and similarly
$\pi_{2} \epsilon'_Q = \overline{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} \pi_2}$.
Hence, by Corollary \ref{cor:srpres}, ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P$ is the plain operad generated by ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P$, satisfying all plain-operadic equations true in $P$.
Since ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}}} P = {\ensuremath{U^{\rm pl}}} {\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P$, the $n$-ary\ operations of ${\ensuremath{U^{\Sigma}_{\rm pl}}} P$ are exactly
the $n$-ary\ operations of $P$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$ be a category with pullbacks, and $T$ be a monad on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Let $(
	\xymatrix{{T}{A} \ar[r]^{a} & {A}}
) \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}^T$.
Let $ \xymatrix{E \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\phi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\phi_2} & TA} $ be the kernel pair of $a$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}$.
Then
\[

	\xymatrix{F_T E \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\bar \phi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\bar \phi_2} & F_T A \ar[r]^-{\epsilon_{(A,a)}} & (A,a) }

\]
is a coequalizer in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}^T$, where $F_T : \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}} \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}^T$ is the free functor, and $\epsilon$ is the counit of the adjunction $F_T \dashv U_T$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
As above.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\index{{\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\Sigma}}}!explicit construction}
Let $P$ be a finite product operad.
Then ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\Sigma}}} P$ is the symmetric operad whose operations are given by those of
$P$, satisfying all linear equations that are true in $P$, and ${\ensuremath{U^{\rm fp}_{\rm pl}}} P$ is the
plain operad whose operations are given by those in $P$, satisfying all
strongly regular equations that are true in $P$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- defn-53: body_md -->
Let $t$ be a $\Phi$-term.
We define a plain-operadic tree $\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t)$ recursively:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $t$ is a variable, let $\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t) = |$.
\item if $t = \phi  (t_1, \dots, t_n)$, let
$\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t) = \phi \circ (\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_1), \dots, \mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_n))$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-53 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:term<->tree}
\index{tree!finite product!equivalence to terms}
Every $\Phi$-term $t$ is equal to $\mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau)$ for a unique finite
product tree $(f\cdot \tau)$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
We will show
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{term->tree->term}
if $t$ is a $\Phi$-term, then $\mathop{\rm{term}}(\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)\cdot \mathop{\rm{tree}}(t)) = t$;
\item
\label{tree->term->tree}
if $(f \cdot \tau)$ is a finite product tree, then
$f = \mathop{\rm{label}}(\mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau))$ and $\tau = \mathop{\rm{tree}}(\mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau))$.
\end{enumerate}

(\ref{term->tree->term}) Let $t$ be a $\Phi$-term.
Let $f = \mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$, and $\tau = \mathop{\rm{tree}}(t)$.
Then $\mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau)$ is $\mathop{\rm{term}}(\tau, (x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(n)}))$.
We proceed by induction.
\begin{itemize}
\item if $t = x_i$, then $\mathop{\rm{term}}(f\cdot \tau)$ is $\mathop{\rm{term}}(|, (x_i))$, which is
$x_i$.
\item if $t = \phi  (t_1, \dots, t_n)$, where each $t_i$ has arity $k_i$,
then
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau) &= &\mathop{\rm{term}}(\phi \circ (\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_1), \dots, \mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_n)),
	(x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(n)})) \\
& = & \phi  (\mathop{\rm{term}}(\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_1), (x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(k_1)})), \dots, \\
& & \phantom{\phi  (} \mathop{\rm{term}}(\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t_n), (x_{f((\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i) + 1)},
		\dots, x_{f(\sum_{i=1}^n k_i)}))) \\
& = & \phi  (t_1, \dots, t_n) \\
& = & t.
\end{eqnarray*}
\end{itemize}

(\ref{tree->term->tree})
Let $\tau$ be an $n$-ary\ plain-operadic tree in $\Phi$, and $f$ a function of
finite sets with codomain ${\underline{m}}$.
Let $t = \mathop{\rm{term}}(f \cdot \tau)$.
We proceed as usual by induction on $\tau$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\tau = |$, then $t = x_{f(1)}$; then $\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t) = | = \tau$ and
$\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$ is the function ${\underline{1}} \to {\underline{m}}$ sending 1 to $f(1)$, i.e. $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)
= f$.
\item If $\tau = \phi \circ (\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n)$, then
\begin{eqnarray*}
t &= &\mathop{\rm{term}}(\phi \circ (\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n), (x_{f(1)},
	\dots, x_{f(\sum k_i)})) \\
&= &\phi (\mathop{\rm{term}}(\tau_1,(x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(k_1)})), \dots,
	\mathop{\rm{term}}(\tau_n, (x_{f((\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i) + 1)}) \dots, 
		x_{f(\sum_{i=1}^n k_i)})))
\end{eqnarray*}
By induction, $\mathop{\rm{var}}(t) = (x_{f(1)}, \dots, x_{f(\sum k_i)})$, so $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t) =
f$, and $\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t) = \phi \circ(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n) = \tau$ as required.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:syntactic_semantic_equiv}
\index{tree!permuted!equivalence to linear terms}
\index{tree!plain-operadic!equivalence to strongly regular terms}
Let $t$ be a $\Phi$-term.
Then $t$ is linear iff $t = \mathop{\rm{term}}(\tau)$ for some permuted tree $\tau$, and
strongly regular iff $t = \mathop{\rm{term}}(\tau)$ for some strongly regular tree $\tau$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
In Lemma \ref{lem:term<->tree}, we factored every $\Phi$-term $t$ into a
strongly regular tree $\mathop{\rm{tree}}(t)$ and a labelling function $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$.
By definition, $t$ is linear iff $\mathop{\rm{label}}(t)$ is a bijection, which occurs iff
$t = \mathop{\rm{term}}(\sigma \cdot \tau)$ for some plain-operadic tree $\tau$ and some
bijection $\sigma$.
Hence, the linear terms and permuted trees are in one-to-one correspondence.
Similarly, strongly regular terms and plain-operadic trees are in one-to-one
correspondence.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:linpresfactor}
Let $(\Phi, E)$ be a presentation of an algebraic theory.
Then $(\Phi, E)$ is linear if and only if the projection maps $ \xymatrix{E \ar@<0.5ex>[r]^-{\pi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[r]_-{\pi_2} & \mathop{\rm{term}}} (\Phi)$ may be factored through the map
$\xymatrix{{\ensuremath{T_{\Sigma}}} \Phi \ar[r]^\eta & {\ensuremath{T_{\rm fp}}} \Phi \ar[r]^{\sim} & \mathop{\rm{term}}{\Phi}}$:
\[
\xymatrix{
E \ar@<0.5ex>[rr]^-{\pi_1} \ar@<-0.5ex>[rr]_-{\pi_2} \unar@<0.5ex>[dr]^-{}
	\unar@<-0.5ex>[dr]_-{}
